ja: ちゅうぎすいこぜんでん

p.src: The Grand Historian said, “The Difficulties of Persuasion and Solitary Indignation were works written when sages and worthies gave vent to their indignation.” From this we may see that the sages and worthies of old wrote nothing unless moved by indignation. To write without indignation is like shivering when one is not cold or groaning when one is not ill—what could be more shameful? Even if such a work were written, what would be worth seeing in it?

p.src: The Water Margin was written to give vent to indignation. For when the house of Song lost its vigor, cap and shoes traded places: men of great worth stood below and the unworthy above, until even the northern tribes stood above and the Central Plain below. Yet the sovereign and ministers of the time were still swallows and sparrows nesting complacently in a hall: they offered tribute, declared themselves vassals, and willingly bent the knee to those they scorned as dogs and sheep! Masters Shi and Luo lived under the Yuan, but their hearts belonged to the Song; though born in the days of the Yuan, they were truly indignant over the affairs of the Song. Thus, indignant at the two emperors being carried captive north, they told of the great defeat of Liao to discharge their anger; and indignant at the makeshift peace after the flight south, they told of the destruction of three rebels to discharge their anger. May I ask who it was that discharged this indignation? They were the very outlaws who had formerly gathered in force at the marsh; one cannot but call them loyal and righteous. For this reason, Masters Shi and Luo, in transmitting the tale of the Water Margin, further entitled their tale “Loyalty and Righteousness.” Why loyalty and righteousness came to reside in the marsh—its cause may readily be understood; but why was every member of the Water Margin band loyal and righteous? The circumstances that drove them there may likewise be understood.

p.src: That lesser virtue should serve greater virtue, and lesser worth serve greater worth, is the natural order. But if a man of little worth commands others while one of great worth is commanded by them, will the latter willingly submit to service without shame? It is like letting the weak bind others while making the strong be bound by them: will the strong willingly fold their hands and submit to bonds without protest? The inevitable result is to drive all the mighty and worthy men under heaven into the Water Margin. It is therefore fair to say that the Water Margin band were all men of great strength and worth, possessed of loyalty and righteousness. Yet none was as loyal and righteous as Song Gongming. The men now numbered as one hundred and eight shared achievement and fault, death and life; their hearts of loyalty and righteousness were like Song Gongming’s own. Song Gongming alone, though dwelling amid the Water Margin, kept his heart fixed upon the imperial court. Intent solely on accepting amnesty and devoted wholly to repaying the country, he ultimately braved great perils, accomplished great deeds, swallowed poison, and hanged himself, refusing to shrink even from sharing death. Such was the ardor of his loyalty and righteousness that it truly sufficed to win the hearts of all one hundred and eight men; thus he could bind them in brotherhood at Mount Liang and become their leader. In the final southern campaign against Fang La, more than half of the one hundred and eight had already fallen in battle. Moreover, Lu Zhishen passed away in meditation at Liuhe, Yan Qing tearfully took leave of his master, and the two lads carried out their stratagem at Hunjiang. It was not that Song Gongming failed to understand their choices; he regarded the wisdom of discerning the opportune moment as no more than a petty man’s scheme for preserving himself, something that one loyal to his sovereign and righteous toward his friends could never stoop to endure. This is what it means to be Song Gongming, and this is why the tale is called “Loyalty and Righteousness.”

p.src: Could such a tale have been left unwritten? Could such a tale be left unread? Thus, a ruler of a state cannot fail to read it. Once he reads this tale, “loyalty and righteousness” will no longer reside in the Water Margin, but all around his sovereign person. A worthy chief minister cannot fail to read it. Once he reads this tale, “loyalty and righteousness” will no longer reside in the Water Margin, but all within the imperial court. The Ministry of War controls the vital machinery of the state’s armed forces, while the military commissions bear sole responsibility for affairs beyond the capital; they too cannot fail to read it. If one day they read this tale, loyalty and righteousness will no longer reside in the Water Margin, but will all become the chosen bulwarks and trusted confidants of the state. Otherwise, if it is not at court, not beside the sovereign, and not among the state’s bulwarks and trusted hearts, where can it be? In the Water Margin. This is the indignation from which the tale was written. As for those fond of anecdotes, they may draw material for conversation from it, while commanders may borrow its stratagems; each merely finds in it what suits his own abilities. How could they ever perceive what is meant by loyalty and righteousness?
